El Ávila National Park occupies the mountain range rising above Caracas. Its forested slopes separate the city valley from the Caribbean coast and form a striking natural backdrop to the capital. From above, you can see dense urban development below and a succession of mountain ridges.

Exploring El Ávila combines an ascent into the mountains with walks and stops at viewpoints. Itineraries use a cable car or road routes through the mountain area. The park offers a chance to see Caracas within its wider natural surroundings and spend part of the journey amid greenery.

## A crater above the capital

El Boquerón National Park lies on the upper slopes of San Salvador Volcano, near [El Salvador's capital](/el-salvador/place/san-salvador/). The main reason to visit is to see the broad volcanic crater with its steep green slopes. A smaller crater, Boqueroncito, sits on its floor and can be viewed from the rim of the larger crater.

## What to see in the park

Marked trails through mountain forest lead to viewpoints. Several observation points offer views of the crater from different angles. The excursion is well suited to a short introduction to volcanic landscapes: a walk along the upper rim does not require descending to the crater floor.

Cafés and restaurants with panoramic views line the approach to the park. This stop can be added to a tour of the capital if the day's itinerary allows.

## El Boquerón on a tour

On the [Best of El Salvador](/el-salvador/tour/el-salvador-san-salvador-suchitoto-gulf-of-fonseca/) itinerary, El Boquerón is visited on the second day, after exploring the historic center of San Salvador. The journey then continues to [Los Volcanes](/el-salvador/place/los-volcanes-national-park/). These are two distinct volcanic areas: El Boquerón reveals the crater above the capital, while the western complex introduces the landscapes of Izalco, Santa Ana and Cerro Verde.

At the edge of the world, amid Patagonia's vast open spaces, lies El Chaltén, a small mountain town often called Argentina's national trekking capital. Here the roads seem to end at the foot of the mountains, and the towering outline of Fitz Roy above the valley becomes the defining landmark.

El Chaltén feels made for travelers who want to do more than see Patagonia: they want to experience it in motion. Numerous hiking trails begin in town, crossing forests and valleys, passing turquoise lakes and winding over rocky mountain passes. One of the most impressive routes leads to Laguna de los Tres, with one of the most recognizable views of the Fitz Roy massif.

Yet El Chaltén is about more than its trails. Small houses, welcoming cafés, mountain panoramas and constantly changing weather create a distinctive way of life. Within a few hours, sunshine over the valley can give way to dramatic clouds gathering above the peaks.

El Chaltén is for those seeking a sense of freedom and a close connection with nature. Here Patagonia is more than a backdrop: it becomes the most memorable part of the entire journey.
